comment:
For those visiting London with a long list of places to see but no idea how to plan it all, this guide is for you. As someone born and raised in London, here's the biggest piece of advice I can give anyone visiting the city. Don't think about London as one giant place. Instead, think about it in two ways:

Geographically – North, South, East, West and Central London. By the TfL transport zones – Zones 1-9, and now combine those two ideas.

A common mistake visitors make is trying to tick off attractions from all over London in the same day. On a map they can look close together, but London is huge. Even Central London is much larger than most people expect, and travelling back and forth across the city wastes valuable time that could be spent actually enjoying it.

Instead, before your trip and heading out each day, decide on one area of London and explore everything nearby. Look at the main attraction you want to visit, then ask yourself, "What else is within walking distance or just a few Tube stops away?" Build your day around that area rather than criss-crossing the city.

To make planning even easier, I like to break Central London into three sections and add in other areas of London: West-Central, Central-Central, East-Central, North London and South London (South of the river).

Although many of London's biggest attractions are in Zone 1 (the city center), it is still enormous. Breaking it into 3 smaller sections makes it much easier to plan your days and helps you discover places you might otherwise miss.

For example, if you're spending the day in West-Central, you could visit Hyde Park, Kensington Palace and the world-famous museums in South Kensington. But instead of heading across London afterwards or back into Central-central (where there are too many things to see), stay in the area and explore nearby neighbourhoods like Notting Hill, Shepherd's Bush (home to Westfield London), or Hammersmith (these are in zones 1-3). You'll not only save time travelling, but you'll also experience parts of London that many tourists never get to see.

The same idea applies wherever you are. Pick an area, explore everything around it, then save the next part of London for another day. You'll spend less time on trains, less time rushing, and far more time actually experiencing the city.

London isn't a city you "complete" in one day—or even one trip. The best way to see it is area by area, letting each neighbourhood tell its own story.

comment:
Firstly, I am in genuine shock. I say this with so much positivity. You are the first American tourist who actually knows how to pronounce certain places/areas (don't get me started on Borough Market pronunciations lol)

To be honest, with the frequency of the buses, tube and national rail/overground services, taxis and Ubers are super expensive in comparison. Speaking of the tube, there are is something called the Daily Cap. How it works is that each zone has its own zonal price (I'll put the links after to help your viewers). So say you are travelling to/from zone 3 to zone 1 (zones 1 and 2 are the same price), once you reach the total around from zone 3 (you can go on the tube as many times as you like within the zones), once you reach the daily cap for zone 3, the rest of the day is free as long as you don't exceed say zones 1 - 3. As for maps and guidance for the tube and buses, I can thoroughly recommend downloading the TFL Go app. You can journey plan, near by buses, the status of all lines and you can also top up your Oyster Card (as long as you register the Oyster Card to the App) via the app. It is also good for those who have mobility needs, they have an option on there for step free travel on the London underground, DLR and the overground services. 

Daily Cap prices - https://content.tfl.gov.uk/adult-fares.pdf
Tube and Overground zonal map - https://content.tfl.gov.uk/london-rail-and-tube-services-map.pdf

The Uber Clippers, especially once it starts to get dark is amazing and costs less than a guided tour on one of the tour boats. Seeing the city from the river Thames and seeing the buildings illuminated is something else and quite magical. This also goes for The London Eye once it goes dark/golden hour. I did the London Eye last December and they had a Christmas theme in the pods. Again, between November and December on the London Eye, you can see some of the attractions and rides at Hyde Park Winter Wonderland from the London Eye (thank you also for NOT calling it a Ferris Wheel; its an Observation wheel ;) ). Also, Abbey Road Studios is not at Abbey Road on the DLR, the closet tube station to Abbey Road is St Johns Wood with the Jubilee and Metropolitan lines. 

Another few greats days out (if theme parks are your thing), going from London Waterloo to Staines is only about 35 mins for Thorpe Park or about 37 mins to Chessington South for Chessington World Of Adventures (next year, they are opening up the worlds first Minecraft World area with some brand new rides). If thrill seeking rides are not your thing and you have younger children, there is also Legoland Windsor. It is 55 mins from London Waterloo (all the 3 attractions are from London Waterloo on the national rail lines) is about 55 mins train journey and then about 29 min journey on a local bus. For something more central to London, Lift 109 is an observation lift at Battersea power station and can be got to via public transport via the Northern Line tube line to Battersea Power Station Station (its a local transport joke within the transport community in the UK) or by the Uber Boats which are once every 30 mins but do check out the Uber Clipper website for that one. 

Merlin Entertainments offer an up to 5 attraction entry ticket (which at the moment in the UK until the start of September is offering a VAT reduction on the ticket prices) for £60.37/$80.30. The more attractions from 1 to 5 on one ticket, the cheaper it gets. the Multi attraction ticket can be used 7 days from the date activated so no need to rush around the 5 attractions it covers. The price I quoted covers Entry to Madame Tussauds, London Eye, SEA LIFE Aquarium, Shrek's Adventure and the London Dungeon and works out at £12.50/$16.62 per person.

How do I know all this... as of the 7th August, I am down for my Birthday Weekend and my at least once a year visit to London. This year, I'm mixing it with my birthday. I am actually considering doing a full room tour and costings whilst down there to help others to like yourself are helping your viewers. Plus, you just got a new sub from me.

comment:
For those visiting London with a long list of places to see but no idea how to plan it all, this guide is for you. As someone born and raised in London, here's the biggest piece of advice I can give anyone visiting the city. Don't think about London as one giant place. Instead, think about it in two ways:

Geographically – North, South, East, West and Central London. By the TfL transport zones – Zones 1-9, and now combine those two ideas.

A common mistake visitors make is trying to tick off attractions from all over London in the same day. On a map they can look close together, but London is huge. Even Central London is much larger than most people expect, and travelling back and forth across the city wastes valuable time that could be spent actually enjoying it.

Instead, before your trip and heading out each day, decide on one area of London and explore everything nearby. Look at the main attraction you want to visit, then ask yourself, "What else is within walking distance or just a few Tube stops away?" Build your day around that area rather than criss-crossing the city.

To make planning even easier, I like to break Central London into three sections and add in other areas of London: West-Central, Central-Central, East-Central, North London and South London (South of the river).

Although many of London's biggest attractions are in Zone 1 (the city center), it is still enormous. Breaking it into 3 smaller sections makes it much easier to plan your days and helps you discover places you might otherwise miss.

For example, if you're spending the day in West-Central, you could visit Hyde Park, Kensington Palace and the world-famous museums in South Kensington. But instead of heading across London afterwards or back into Central-central (where there are too many things to see), stay in the area and explore nearby neighbourhoods like Notting Hill, Shepherd's Bush (home to Westfield London), or Hammersmith (these are in zones 1-3). You'll not only save time travelling, but you'll also experience parts of London that many tourists never get to see.

The same idea applies wherever you are. Pick an area, explore everything around it, then save the next part of London for another day. You'll spend less time on trains, less time rushing, and far more time actually experiencing the city.

London isn't a city you "complete" in one day—or even one trip. The best way to see it is area by area, letting each neighbourhood tell its own story.

It's also free (although there might be a charge for special exhibits) and is way more manageable and engaging.  Not just stuffy old portraits, but lots of contemporary works of familiar subjects.  While in that area, pop right across the street to St. Martin-in-the-Fields for a look at their lovely sanctuary and perhaps view a free concert.  You can also grab a relatively inexpensive lunch at Café in the Crypt below the church.
